He rose to the peak of his profession, of course, at a time when there were many personal jealousies against him.
Many remember the phrase that is associated with Coppee, that he did not lack the French Academy but the French Academy lacked Coppee. I am quite prepared to draw culturally from people of this reputation no matter what part of the world they come from. I think of Rembrandt, Constable, Van Gogh. Yet we are told that one must say that in cultural matters a country cannot continually live by borrowing its material from others. I for one am quite content to borrow my material from the sources I have just mentioned, and I do not think there is a man in the house who would quarrel with that statement. But no, we must go and throw $10 million into the pot to develop a feature film industry, when we know that the feature film industry is in the poorest financial shape today in the world that it has ever been. Hollywood is only a quarter of what is used to be. The attendance for films is not one quarter of what it used to be before the advent of television. But this is the time that Canada should leap into the breach, and let us Canadians show the rest of the world that when the tide is against us we will swim against the tide.
We are told by the hon. member for Outrement-Saint-Jean that Canadians seem to have been unable to bring forth a film industry in Canada which could find its inspiration in a Canadian setting and produce and distribute a Canadian-made product. The Secretary of State stated this afternoon that, because of the geographical position of this country, the divisions into which it falls and the linguistic separations, it was difficult to establish a feature film industry in this dominion, and that the government should endeavour to help it become established. If I noted one of the statements correctly, it was that we should be under no illusion about the difficulties Canadian film producers are going to have to face in establishing the industry.
I also say, let there be no illusion in this respect. Let us realize that this is an industry into which the Canadian government should not be pouring $10 million at this time. If there is a possibility of the industry's being established in this country, I have enough confidence in free enterprise and the private investors to believe that they would have established such an industry if there was an opening for it.

The former secretary of state, as I mentioned, spoke in Montreal on August 5, 1964. I shall be making further references to those remarks. Under date of August 10, 1964, we have the Montreal Star writing an editorial the heading of which is, "Government In Show Biz?" The article says:
Mr. Lamontagne's announcement of a loan fund to assist the production of feature films in Canada puts the government in show biz, notoriously the most risky form of artistic enterprise . . .
We hope this will include a study of the fact that nobody knows what a big film will be like until it is written, directed, produced, and the money spent. Then outlets for distribution are needed before the cash registers begin ringing in the box office. Very many people have gone broke in show biz. A few people and a few film companies have made a packet.
Then continues the Montreal Star:
But let's ask who is going to pay to see them and where? The Canadian market is small and divided culturally and linguistically.
The movie houses are mainly tied tight to the big Hollywood companies. Will they be prepared to show the Canadian-made films? This should be included in the proposed study of the loan fund which otherwise will find all its money going out and nothing coming back.
Then following the remarks made by the member for Outremont-Saint-Jean the Toronto Globe and Mail on August 8, 1964, had an article headed, "Money to Burn?" This article said:
Canada's taxpaying public may well be disturbed by the Pearson government's announcement, made through State Secretary Maurice Lamontagne, that it intends later in the session "to ask parliament for the necessary authority to establish a loan fund to assist in the production of feature films of high quality in Canada".
The production of feature films, and especially those of high quality, is a most expensive, and most uncertain, business. Millions of dollars have been lost in it, sometimes on a single picture. Has the Pearson government, have the Canadian people, so much money that they can start pouring it into the making of full-length movies?
The article continues:
Mr. Lamontagne's announcement was accompanied by two interesting developments elsewhere. The Commons public accounts committee expressed concern-and properly so-at the rapidly mounting cost of new facilities sought by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in Montreal and Toronto.
It goes on to talk about the mounting cost of the C.B.C. Consider this. This is supposed to be the first step in establishing a feature film industry and it will cost $10 million. We have a hole in the ground at the corner of Sparks and Elgin that was originally to cost $9 million when completed. We have the hole in the ground, and we are now told we will

Development of Film Industry be able to complete it for $31 million. This is the estimate for the National Arts Centre.
If the artistic world's estimate for this theatrical centre was $9 million and it has now gone up to $31 million, figure what $10 million will be by the time we get our necks caught in the wringer of the feature film industry. It will be somewhere around $35 million, and I would prophesy that the end is not yet come. The Globe and Mail continues in its article of August 8, 1964:
If the C.B.C. (which does a lot of moviemaking) is so expensive to maintain, and if members of all parties are disturbed at the amount it requires, why is the Canadian government going into another money-devouring venture?
Then it says:
Government assistance, whether in loans or subsidies-or loans that turn into subsidies- is the wrong way to go at it. The government should let Canada's feature film industry develop itself, in its own way, with its own money. If there is room for it, it needs no help. If there is not room for it, all the tax dollars in Ottawa will be of no help to it.

The subject seems to have lain quiescent for a time from August 1964; and then, on April 5, 1965, the following words appeared in the Speech from the Throne: "and a measure to help the development of a feature film industry in Canada". Those few words brought on another flood of editorial comment, some of which I believe should be read at this time when we are being given the first opportunity to discuss this matter in a serious vein.
On April 7, 1965, two days after the Speech from the Throne, the Ottawa Citizen, which is reputed to have an "in" with the cabinet, published an item headed "A subsidized Film Industry", and reading as follows:
Judging by the Speech from the Throne, the government evidently will go ahead with its intention to help the Canadian film industry, presumably through some form of subsidy. When the legislation is introduced, it deserves the closest and most critical possible examination in parliament. For on the face of it the plan is ill-conceived, and the merits of the government's proposal will have to be demonstrated to the hilt before a penny of public funds is appropriated for this scheme . . .
During her visit here recently, Mrs. Indira Gandhi, a member of the Indian government, expressed doubts that India's experiment in subsidizing a domestic film industry had been successful in terms of quality-
I am referring to this because Mrs. Gandhi referred to the quality of feature films which is the subject matter of this resolution. There is nothing cheap about the films we intend to develop; they have to be feature films. Mrs.

Gandhi says that in subsidizing the domestic film industry India has not been successful in producing quality films. The article goes on to say:
Certainly, the scheme had succeeded in terms of quantity. But the government has found itself subsidizing mediocrity and sensationalism.
The Citizen goes on to say:
On the other hand, is the Canadian government to begin supervising the quality of the commercially produced films it subsidizes? That would make the federal government virtually a censor and a producer in the commercial field. Surely public funds could be put to better use than that.
Parliament was dissolved in September of 1965 and we had a new election on our hands. In October a meeting of the Canadian Conference of the Arts took place in Toronto. The Globe and Mail of October 14, 1965 made reference to it in an article headed: "Lain ontagne Announces Crown Corporation; Film Industry to get $10,000,000 Ottawa Aid" and stating:
The Canadian government will establish a Crown corporation with an initial capital of $10 million, to assist the Canadian private film industry in the production of feature films.
Maurice Lamontagne, Secretary of State, told a luncheon meeting of the Canadian Conference of the Arts in the Royal York hotel yesterday that the films should be "of commercial value and good quality".
He added that he hopes that within a short period of time the Canadian film industry will prove to be a $50 million a year industry-

The report in the Globe and Mail continues;
The corporation, Mr. Lamontagne said in his speech, "will be empowered to make agreements with private producers under which it will make loans or investments without, however, becoming a legal partner".

I rise to express my support for the spirit and purpose of this resolution. I have listened with great interest to the speech which has just been made by the hon. member for York-Humber, in which he informed the house that hon. members on the government side are told very little by the cabinet. Later on he said hon. members on the government side of the house were never told in advance what was to happen in the house, that it takes occasions such as these for these secrets to leak out.
However, I do not think that is a valid argument against the resolution. His argument was based on the fact that he had apparently written to persons who are naturally anxious to get an increase in their old age pensions to ask them whether they would rather have an increase from $75 to $100 a month, or see the establishment of a feature film board. All of us could write such letters. Naturally in the majority of cases the reply would be that these people would rather have an increase in their pay cheques, because that is what people want at this time. There is no relationship between the amount of expenditure required by this government to increase pensions and the amount required to form this board. It is just the same as when we in this house get up day after day and complain that the government is spending $5 million or $10 million on a public building that is required. I do not think that is a valid argument.
While I have always realized that the member for York-Humber is an honourable gentleman who on some occasions expresses his point of view without fear or favour-and on some occasions I have agreed with him -I must say that on this occasion I simply cannot accept his line of reasoning, his argument or his approach to this question. I think he failed to appreciate the fact that this, similarly to other legislation which we have passed in recent days, is somewhat in the nature of an experiment. He fails to appreciate what can be done along these lines if it is pursued in a sound manner. I might say at this point that I do not claim to be a cultured person, but I am always inclined to

speechtext:
As one of those who have been directly interested in the motion picture industry in this country for some years, I thought I should like to make a few comments this evening concerning the introduction of this measure to establish a corporation known as the Canadian Film Development Corporation. Like all hon. members of this house, I am in favour of the further development of the arts and culture in our country. I am looking forward to the time when Canada can establish its own identity in Canadian literature, music, art and other things cultural.
However, I have some grave doubts about this resolution so far as the development of a feature film industry in this country at this time is concerned. In the first place, $10 million is a paltry amount in relation to a job of this kind. It is like sending a boy to do a man's errand. Hollywood is the centre of the United States film industry, and with the vast millions that have been put into it, that industry has run into grave difficulties in the last few years. The reason for this has been the impact of television. Television has cut very deeply into this private industry to the extent that in Canada-I have not got the exact figures-hundreds of theatres have had to close their doors. I know that in Winnipeg, the gateway to the west, as a result of the impact of television, no less than 11 theatres closed down in one year.
This does not mean that I am injecting a gloomy note into our discussion. There is still room for motion picture production. However, I feel we have to look at the matter carefully in a young country like Canada that has many more important responsibilities at this time to which reference has been made. It is a curious fact that the minister recently suggested paying $6 million for one painting, but now she suggests an amount of only $10


million for the establishment of a motion picture industry.
The motion picture industry, for instance, is divided into four main branches. First, there are the stars. A few years ago the cost of these stars did not run into too big an item because the motion picture producer could hire a top star on an annual contract. As a result, he might be able to produce anywhere from five to ten pictures with the one star. Now these motion picture stars of top calibre insist on getting into the production end before they will even lend their talents to a production. They usually insist on a contract under which they will make only one or two pictures a year and will take a large share of the profits, sometimes 50 per cent. I do not believe Canada would be in a different position if we were to establish a motion picture industry.
We would find ourselves in the same difficulties as private industry has in this regard. Then, too, these production companies with unlimited millions of dollars behind them have, in the last several years, found it necessary to amalgamate in order to remain in business. Then, you have distribution which is a very important part of the whole motion picture industry. It is all right to produce a picture, but you have to have a whole chain of distribution centres in order to get this film to the next stage, which is the exhibitor himself. All in all, Mr. Chairman, I think we should take a very serious look at this resolution before we support it 100 per cent.
For instance, I think the hon. member for Saskatoon mentioned that back in 1948-I recall reading about this-Mr. J. Arthur Rank, one of the great producers of England, came to Canada to look at the potential of this country for the motion picture industry. I must remind you this was before the advent of television and its impact on the motion picture industry. This top executive from that great country came to the conclusion that we were too young, and we did not have a large enough population to support a motion picture industry. He withdrew from Canada, and I believe we should learn a lesson from that action. I just wanted to voice this note of warning to the minister, Mr. Chairman. This government project, even though it may sound laudable, could prove to be a boomerang if we do not give it serious consideration.

I should like to say a few words on this resolution. Frankly I must tell the minster that I feel this resolution, at this time, is ill considered. The sum of $10 million which is involved in starting a new venture could be used in many other ways by existing cultural establishments. I am speaking of our live theatre, our ballets and our symphony orchestras. We hear from the Canada Council that there is a shortage of funds to meet their requirements. We know that television is the strongest medium of communication we have today, yet we do not have very much Canadian developed programs in that industry. One can think of "Seaway" which was Canadian developed, and then one is at a loss to think of any others except perhaps "Milk and Honey". We do have some Canadian television, but there is not very much.
I suggest that rather than start a venture with such an uncertain future at this time, if the government has $10 million to be used it could be used to develop Canadian talent. It could be channelled into cultural establishments which exist now and which are suffering because of a shortage of funds.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
It seems to me that if we have this sort of money to invest at the present time we should give more encouragement to our television industry and enable them to increase the scope of their enterprise, which would be more rewarding than trying to make feature films which, at best, are products with a very uncertain future and for which we do not appear to have any definite market.
I also suggest to the minister that there are already under way centennial projects which were instigated by this government but which have now run short of funds owing to the inflationary pressures and increased costs which have been brought about by the policies of this government. Yet the government now refuses to increase the supply of funds and enable completion of these projects.
Development of Film Industry
I think it would be strange indeed if this house were to vote an expenditure of $10 million for a feature film industry when there are steel skeletons of centennial projects in various parts of the country which are supposed to serve the cultural interests of the country. We have live theatre and other establishments already in existence, but we have insufficient funds to complete these projects. The government now washes its hands of any further responsibility and tells the municipalities, if you please, that these projects are now their baby and they should go ahead and do what they can with them.
We have in Ottawa what is referred to as the "hole" in "confusion square", the cost of which started out at $9 million. I referred to this in a question to the minister the other day. Now the cost is, not $31 million, but I understand that $34 million is the probable cost of completion of this project; and for this the government must take full responsibility.
However, let me get away from Ottawa. As I say the steel for these projects is lying on site because no funds are available to complete the projects in time for centennial year. The minister says that the government has given $2.5 million; that these projects are now the municipalities' baby.
It seems to me that it would look very peculiar if we started to develop a feature film industry with an initial expenditure of $10 million-and God knows what the cost will escalate to-while we leave these skeletons on view. This steel is lying on the ground, of no possible use, at a time when perhaps $10 million at the outside would enable the people who accepted these projects, and who started to develop them in all good faith, to complete them. In view of the time clause placed by the government in the contracts for completion in 1967, these people went ahead with their plans but now find them stalled.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that rather than this highfalutin interest in a feature film industry, the minister should look at the present centennial programs which are under way but which remain unfinished owing to lack of funds. I suggest she should devote this $10 million to the completion of a program which has already been started.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution and bill presently before the committee breaks new ground in agricultural legislation for Canada. It is the first bill that will provide a legislative base for the establishment of a commission with Canada-wide responsibility for an agricultural commodity.
One of the major problems of the Canadian dairy industry, a problem common to dairy industries in all countries and in fact to agricultural production of almost all types, is the cyclical nature of production patterns and, with it, price instability. While the length of the cycle may vary from product to product, the cycles have common characteristics: a period of high production coupled with falling prices; then a period of readjustment which often results in excessive curtailment of production and subsequent high prices. This period seems to be inevitably followed by surging production induced by the high prices, which in turn generate consumer resistance and decreased consumption. And so the cycle starts anew.
Many devices have been and are being used to meet this problem. Paramount among these are support measures and rational marketing. Earlier this year a major change in the government's approach to dairy support was announced. This announcement

represented the first stage in the government's dairy program. Under it, shippers of manufacturing milk will receive direct payments from the government of 75 cents per hundredweight, which will result in a national average return of $4 per hundredweight for 3.5 per cent milk, f.o.b. the factory. An equivalent payment will be made to shippers of farm-separated cream.
This program was implemented because producer income from dairying was such that there had been a sharp cutback in production. In other words, the production cycle was approaching the stage where curtailed production and high consumer prices would result. The program has been in effect only since April of this year and production patterns in the dairy industry change slowly. But it is of interest to note that figures for the month of May indicate that the downward trend in butter production has been curtailed, restoring a measure of stability to this product.
The second phase of the government's dairy program is the establishment of a Canadian Dairy Commission, and perhaps it would be useful at this point to review briefly some of the events leading to the development of this legislation.
In 1963 the Canadian dairy industry was plagued with low prices and surpluses. At that time a meeting was called at which the various segments of the industry, both producer and processor, as well as federal and provincial governments, were represented. The conference agreed that the forming of a body or organization to perform a co-ordinated and advisory function for the dairy industry was a requirement. The conference recommended that a co-ordinating and advisory committee called the Canadian dairy advisory committee be established with representation from the various groups. Subsequently this committee met on many occasions. Subject matters covered by the committee included research, dairy quality and marketing. A basic recommendation in the latter category was that a national dairy authority be developed.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
On March 26, 1965, when the dairy support program for the forthcoming year was announced, the announcement included a statement that it was the intention of the government to introduce legislation to provide for a Canadian Dairy Commission. Many groups, including the Dairy Farmers of Canada and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, have
June 20, 1966	COMMONS
supported, by means of briefs and submissions, this intention.
Under our constitution, the responsibility for agricultural production and for marketing controls lies largely with the provinces. However, when agricultural commodities cross interprovincial or international boundaries, federal authority is involved.
With the growing complexity and sophistication of marketing techniques in this country, very often it is not known when a product is produced or processed whether its ultimate destination shall be within the province of production or elsewhere in the country. With this development in marketing procedures, there has been increasing need for legislation to complement that of the provinces in order to ensure orderly marketing procedures.
The bill that I shall introduce this evening will establish a commission, one of the primary functions of which will be, in co-operation with provincial agencies, the co-ordination of such marketing matters.
This commission will also have authority to administer the dairy support program, to engage in the promotion of dairy products and in general to take such action as will result in the development of a dairy industry best suited to the needs of the country. The commission will consist of three members appointed by the governor in council and will have available the services of a consultative committee of nine members. It is the intention that members will be representative of the various segments of the dairy industry in Canada.
In order that it may meet its objectives, funds will be provided to the commission from three sources. First, the amounts required for the implementation of the federal dairy support program will be provided to it under the provisions of the Agricultural Stabilization Act; second, the amounts required for the commission's own administrative operations will be provided to it by a vote of parliament and, third, the commission will be empowered to raise funds through levies and licences.
While the commission will be able to perform any provincial function that might be delegated to it under provincial legislation, it should be stressed that one of its major roles will be to work in co-ordination and co-operation with provincial boards in meeting its objectives.	*
It is not possible at this time to indicate, other than in a broad way, the manner in

Stabilization of Milk and Cream Prices which the commission will operate. The dairy industry is a complex and ever changing entity, and with these changes, different approaches will doubtless be needed on the part of the commission.
The legislation has been drafted to provide for sufficient flexibility to permit the commission to meet the objectives set for it, despite changing structures in the Canadian dairy industry. A healthy agriculture in Canada must be predicated on assurance to producers of returns commensurate with their labours and with their contribution to society, and equivalent returns to other segments of the population. In recent years this has not been the case.
Broad government agricultural policy toward this end is on a three fold basis. First, producers must be able to establish efficient and viable production units. Here government action has been taken through upward revisions in the funds available under the Farm Credit Act and through the introduction of the Farm Machinery Syndicates Credit Act. Complementary to this is the ARDA program that in essence will provide for those unable, for whatever reason it may be, to develop a viable production entity.
The second cornerstone for an efficient agriculture must be that of marketing. Production, no matter how efficient it may be by itself, cannot stand alone and is useless, unless the fruits of production are marketed at a price commensurate with their costs. The present legislation represents a very significant step in this latter direction. No matter how efficient production may be, or how well marketing may be conducted, the agricultural producer still requires protection against losses beyond his control.
Despite the advances we have made in technology, little or no protection is possible against the vagaries of the weather. Herein lies the role of crop insurance. Already the government has made a significant change in the legislation through an amendment providing for re-insurance of a portion of the province's risk. The results of this change have been a very significant increase in the utilization of this federal act, and thus in the protection provided to producers.
I suggest that in these three areas lies the importance to the general well being of the economics of the agricultural community, towards which the objectives of this government in an agricultural sense will be directed. In speaking in support of this resolution, Mr. Chairman, I intend to confine my remarks to explaining the reasons and the necessity for the type of amendments which will be proposed in the bill and to give a general outline of the matters to be dealt with. I shall be prepared to go into the matter in considerably more detail when the bill comes before the house for second reading.
Hon. members will recall that the Crop Insurance Act was passed in 1959 to permit the Minister of Agriculture, with the approval of the governor in council, to enter into agreements with any province to make contributions to the administrative costs incurred by the province in the operation of an insurance scheme and to provide 20 per cent of the amount of the premiums which would be necessary to make the insurance program self-sustaining. Under the original legislation three provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Prince Edward Island, entered into

The bill also provides, as I have mentioned-and this should encourage participation by the provinces, and it should encourage participation by individual farmers-for an increase in the federal contribution to premiums from 20 to 25 per cent.
As I have indicated, I shall be prepared to discuss these amendments in detail when the bill is before the house. I trust hon. members will give their favourable consideration to the resolution at this stage.
I would also point out that the amendments proposed provide for insurance coverage which will reimburse a farmer for costs incurred in preparing summerfallow which the farmer could not seed in the normal seeding season because of excessive moisture. The bill provides for extended coverage of this type to be provided in agreement with a province.
There are two other minor amendments which I shall not mention at this time; they can be dealt with on second reading. Before closing I should like to express my concern about some remarks which have been made in connection with crop insurance in recent weeks. There have been suggestions that the present act does not provide for spot coverage on individual crops. This is interpreted to mean that under the present federal legislation a province cannot produce a program which will provide for the settlement of claims other than on an entire farm or an entire crop basis. While it is true that present programs in effect in the prairie provinces make it compulsory to insure all of a specific crop and provide only for indemnities on the basis of the entire acreage seeded to that crop, the federal act does not in fact prohibit the issuance of insurance which would provide indemnities on the basis of losses pertaining to a portion of that crop or with respect to selected fields. It would, however, seem evident that premium rates based on spot settlement would possibly be much higher than those based on the loss related to the entire acreage seeded to any crop on any farm.
There has been some criticism, too, that the federal act does not provide coverage for forage crops such as corn, hay and pasture. In actual fact, the act places no limitation on the crops which may be covered and defines the term crop as meaning an agricultural crop declared by the regulations to be a crop for the purposes of the scheme. Members on this side of the house have certainly listened with interest to the Minister of Agriculture introducing this resolution on the subject of crop insurance. We can well appreciate the reason the government has been placed in the position once again of having to amend this particular piece of farm legislation. For many years all major farm groups have been advocating that crop insurance be provided to each farmer on a basis which would afford him recompense for losses due to nature.
The fact that so few farmers have so far taken advantage of the Crop Insurance Act, even though four provinces have now agreed to accept the principles and work it out with the federal government, indicates that amendments were needed. The fact remains that farmers still did not feel that this measure provided the necessary protection. As a result they have not been taking full advantage of the crop insurance provisions even though, as was pointed out by the minister, by the 1964 amendment the federal government did agree to pay 20 per cent of the farm premiums.
Farmers today are keen businessmen. If something were offered to them as a bargain, the government paying 20 per cent of the premiums, they would certainly investigate it thoroughly. Nevertheless farm groups in Ontario, after investigating the farm credit insurance provisions put forward by this government, did not feel they could recommend to the provincial government that full advantage be taken of this particular measure.
I was interested tonight to hear the Minister of Agriculture say he had held consultations with various provincial ministers of agriculture and that this subject had been discussed in depth. I have no doubt it is because of these meetings and because of the views expressed by the provincial ministers that the amendments of which the minister spoke tonight are to be incorporated in the new legislation.
I hope that these meetings have been responsible for amendments to the act which will make the legislation adequate to provide for the losses which can be expected every year in some part of every province of Canada.

June 20. 1966
Crop Insurance Act
I am sure that because of the nature of the special crops grown in many parts of this country, the 60 per cent coverage of the long-term average was one of the stumbling blocks against a greater adoption of this particular insurance plan. I am pleased to note that the minister speaks of increasing this coverage to 80 per cent of the average yield.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
I think farmers on the whole agree with this principle of spot settlement because in many instances when hail, drought or rust strike they do not affect a whole farm. The loss is confined to one particular part or section but the insurance is placed on a complete district, thus providing little recompense for an individual farmer.
The house is going to be seized of and intrigued by the minister's proposition that forage crops will be contemplated as ones to be covered by the policy, and I can see many problems evolve from this move on the part of the government. Certainly it is desirable, but a tremendous amount of work will have to be done to provide a practical method of estimating the actual loss, estimating the average crop, and determining whether or not 80 per cent or more of the crop has been damaged.
The minister also spoke of insurance to cover what he called production units. This will deal with fruit trees and other more intensified types of farming. Grape arbours, berry patches and staked tomatoes, and presumably various other high cost crops will come under this. I hope enough preliminary work has been done in this field so that an equitable premium can be established to make it possible for the producers of these high cost crops to take full advantage of crop insurance, and for the first time place them in a position where they can receive some recompense for the vagaries of nature that often cause them maximum monetary loss.
The fact that crop insurance has been implemented in only four provinces leads me to the next question as to whether, at his conference with the provincial ministers, the Minister of Agriculture was able to obtain an assurance that the provincial governments which have not yet applied this particular offer from the federal government will undertake to review the situation. I am speaking in particular of provinces like Quebec and Ontario. I hope they are interested enough in this crop insurance legislation to feel it can be utilized for their farmers.

I am rather concerned over the fact that there was an increase from 20 per cent to 25 per cent in the premium offer by the federal government. When this legislation was introduced I was interested to know why the figure of 20 per cent was chosen in the first place, and I found that this figure did not seem to entice many farmers to enter into this particular insurance policy. Now I wonder what is the basic reason behind the government's raising it from 20 per cent to 25 per cent.
Surely if farmers were not enamoured of the program at 20 per cent, an additional 5 per cent is not going to make much difference. On the other hand, certainly farmers are not going to turn it down, but it is food for thought why the government raised it just 5 per cent rather than 10 per cent or 15 per cent. Was this done on the advice of provincial ministers who felt it would make it a more successful insurance policy, or did the government have another reason?
I am not going to deal at length with the resolution tonight. The government has taken what farm orgnizations across the country felt was a necessary step. Something has been drastically wrong with the crop insurance program introduced by the federal government. I think all hon. members realize that basically it was not acceptable to the majority of the farmers. It is most necessary, especially in view of the growing costs which farmers are faced with today. But the fact that they did not adopt it universally leads one to consider that the plan in itself left much to be desired.
We shall look forward to reading the bill with real and sincere interest, and we hope the minister will then take all the time he desires to answer in detail many of the questions that will arise with regard to the manner in which the different provisions are going to be set up, the way they are to be administered, and the manner in which the various regulations and qualifications will be established as standards. A lot will have to be explained with regard to this bill, which is extending into a brand new field. It is a field of utmost importance to agriculture, and we on this side sincerely hope that for once the government has brought forth something that will be practical and workable and to the advantage of the Canadian farmer.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, twice within recent weeks I have attempted to ask the government
June 20, 1966
whether consideration was being given at cabinet level to the proposition of increasing the old age security pension by the payment of a bonus. On those occasions, Mr. Speaker, you ruled my questions out of order. In consequence I am raising it again at this late evening sitting.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
The reason behind my question can best be found in a quotation from a news story which appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail on June 11 and which reads as follows:
Strong pressure is developing among Liberal M.P.'s, including some cabinet ministers, for special action to assist old persons who will not benefit from the Canada Pension Plan.
The government is being urged to set up a special fund to supplement the basic $75 a month old age pension. The fund would decline as the benefits paid under the Canada Pension Plan rose over the next 10 years. This plan may be introduced late this year or next year when inflationary pressures ease off.
The government had resisted efforts by the opposition parties in the Commons to raise old age pensions to $100 a month. But an increasing number of Liberal members, led by cabinet ministers, are arguing that something must be done to aid old folk.
The reported consideration being given by the cabinet to a bonus for old age pensioners is a very welcome one, if it is indeed a fact. We can only hope that, failing a general increase in the pension rate to $100 a month-which many hon. members would like to see-a practical step would be the immediate provision of a supplementary amount in the form of a bonus. This would at least make up part of that increase in the cost of living which the old age pensioners have felt very sharply in the last three years.
In asking whether the government is actually considering such a provision I wish to add a cautionary note. In the event that a bonus will be paid we hope it will not be done at the expense of the Canada Pension Plan. We think that the Canada Pension Plan should not be siphoned off by reducing it to augment the old age pensions. We believe it is possible to increase the current old age pension security by making money available without taking it from the Canada Pension Plan or from increased taxation.
It seems to us that the government has leeway in the economies it could practise to provide the proposed bonus to old age pensioners. For example I understand that approximately $2 million a day is being spent on national defence and that something like $1 million is being spent in simply paying the interest portion of the federal debt.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
We think that if the government will take measures, as we hope it will, to improve the old age pension by providing a bonus, then it should not do so at the expense of another plan which provides for old age pensioners or people who will benefit from the new pension plan. We think that the government should face up to the fact that there is a gap between the present old age pension and the new contributory one, and it should move ahead to fill that gap on a national basis.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that at least in my view today's old age pensioners are probably the last people to remain in the valley of scarcity. Thanks to their work in bygone days the rest of us are emerging into a world of abundance, and I think it is fitting for us at this time to recognize the need of our older people by the provision of this bonus. I therefore wish to ask the government to consider such a move.
Mrs. Margaret Rideout (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health
and Welfare): Answers to similar questions can be found on pages 6122 and 6434 of Hansard. I am sure the hon. member will realize after reading these detailed replies by the minister that there is very little I can add to what has already been said.
I should like to reiterate, however, some of the major points the minister made in dealing with those questions. I want to point out that in the current fiscal year, 1966-67 federal expenditures in respect of old age security will amount to $1,035 billion. It should be pointed out also that in 1963-64 the federal government was spending $755 million on old age security payments. This means that in a period of three years outlays have been increased by $280 million or 37 per cent. During this period of three years the level or rate of benefit has been raised and the number of persons covered has been increased by 100,000 through the lowering of the age threshold to 69 on January 1, 1966.
I think the hon. member for New Westminster will agree that it is impressive to note, as the minister did when discussing his estimates before the health and welfare committee, that 28 per cent of the federal government's expenditures are directed toward the health and welfare of the Canadian people. The largest single component of that is for our older citizens. Moreover, as my hon. friend knows the Canada Pension Plan is intended to be a long term solution to retirement support for the wage earners of Canada.

The Liberal party has always been on record in support of increased assistance to old age pensioners. I believe that we have gone a long way during the past three years toward the achievement of our aim. We have in effect today a substantially more generous and much broader program for old age security recipients than was in effect when this government took office in 1963.

I should like, at the outset, to express my appreciation of the action of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in his seconding the question I raised this afternoon concerning the case of one Masako Endo, who had travelled from Japan to Canada with the intention of visiting here but who ran afoul of the immigration authorities in Vancouver. Apparently a deportation order has been issued to return her to Japan with her visit uncompleted.
Now, as one who has twice visited Japan, I am familiar first hand with the unfailing courtesy of immigration officials there. I know that on my second visit I made an error upon entering the country and failed to

DEBATES	June 20, 1966
declare a trunk which arrived the next day. I suppose a deportation order could have been issued against me and I would have been sent immediately from the country. However, it was possible to talk to the officials and explain my oversight. I then completed a six month visit there. I know as well the concern of the people of that country for visitors from any land.
A Canadian girl who was visiting there at the same time I was happened to have her handbag stolen on the streets of Tokyo. The incident was reported in the Tokyo newspapers. Within a matter of two weeks she had received letters from all over the country, several handbags and more money than she had lost. People were concerned that a visitor should have been treated in a manner which they felt was unworthy of their country.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
It was with some of the same feeling that I read the report in the newspaper this morning that this particular person expecting to visit Canada had been treated in such a heavy-handed manner by the immigration officials in Vancouver. Certainly if the government of Japan chose to reply in kind, I am sure that each year some hundreds of young Canadian visitors to Japan would be deported summarily. I know a great many Canadian visitors who go to Japan on visitors' visas engage in employment by teaching English to Japanese students. I happened to be one of them when I was there on my last visit. I am sure that if the Japanese applied the full measure of the law to all of these visitors, deportations would occur and be enforced. Fortunately they have taken a little more enlightened view, it would seem, than that which is taken by the immigration authorities in Vancouver.
It seems to me that this is a particularly unhappy moment for this type of publicity. This is the time when the summer tourist season is about to begin, a time when our visitors from Japan are increasing in number. They are an important source of revenue to the province of British Columbia and this country and they form an important cultural link with this Pacific nation. Should this sort of publicity reach Japan I am sure there would be consternation in the minds of a great many Japanese who had planned to visit this country.
Again, it is most unfortunate that this has occurred at a time when an immigration office has been opened in the city of Tokyo. I can think of nothing which would work more
June 20, 1966	COMMONS
against our professed desire to encourage immigration from this land than the sort of incident that has been reported in the paper. Even allowing for some exaggeration on the part of the press regarding the detention into which Miss Endo was placed by immigration officials, it should be remembered that she was barely able to speak English and would not be able to offer a full explanation to the immigration authorities.
I do not know just what the problem is here, whether the situation will require a change in personnel at Vancouver or simply a request from the department that a little more reasonable attitude be taken. We try to tighten down, I suppose, in the hope that the Hal Banks and the Munsingers will be kept out of the country; but all we succeed in doing is catching the most harmless people and subjecting them to what seems to me to be a totally unnecessary harassment.
I hope that this deportation order will be rescinded when the appeal is heard. I am amazed it has to be heard at all. It seems to me that if there is provision for a three-month visitation and a visitor wished to stay an extra month at the end of those three months, there should be some machinery whereby she could apply for an extension of one month and the matter could be dealt with in that way, instead of immediately issuing a deportation order, which once issued must apparently be heard, with the whole visit being placed under a cloud of uncertainty as to what is going to happen. I also hope that there will be some expression from the department to the officials in Vancouver to

Mr. Speaker, by way of reply to the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke, I would inform him that we have endeavoured to obtain a report from the officials in Vancouver. All we know at the present time seems to indicate that this young lady arrived on Friday, June 17 and was referred to an immigration special inquiry on the next day, Saturday, June 18. It would seem she did not have a visa when she arrived here.
I am certain that immigration officials really had no choice in the matter. I do not think they had any ambit for discretion. The young lady did not have a visa, and the only course open to the immigration officials, under our act, is to refer the matter to a special inquiry. I understand that has been held.
The young lady entered an appeal which will be considered within the next few days. There is no indication that there was any heavy-handed display toward her by our immigration officials in Vancouver. We certainly hope there was not. We again reiterate that there is no ambit for discretion when somebody comes to the country without a visa, which is the case at the moment. We shall try to obtain more facts and have them available as soon as possible.
